li.p: {11\choose 7}= {330}\text{.} Note that a strictly increasing function is automatically injective. So the 7 outputs must all be different. So lets first pick which 7 outputs we will use: there are {11 \choose 7} ways to do this. Now how many ways are there to assign those outputs to the inputs 1 through 7? Only one way, since there is only one way to arrange numbers in increasing order.

{17 \choose 7}\text{.} This is in fact a sticks and stones problem. The stones are the 7 inputs, and the sticks are the 10 spots between the 11 possible outputs. Think of it this way: We will specify f(1)\text{,} then f(2)\text{,} then f(3)\text{,} and so on in that order. Start with the possible output 0. We can use it as the output of f(1)\text{,} or we can switch to 1 as a potential output. Say we put f(1) = 1\text{.} Now we are at 1 (cant go back to 0). Should f(2) = 1\text{?} If yes, then we are putting down another stone. If no, put down a bar and switch to 2. Maybe you switch to 3, then assign f(2) = 3 and f(3) = 3 (two more stones) before switching to 4 as a possible output. And so on.
